title: AMD's Lisa Su, in Taipei, commits to a substantial 2027 chip supply increase
subtitle: The CEO told reporters AMD will extend joint capacity planning with its Asian suppliers from one or two years to three to five, citing agentic AI as a driver of unmet CPU and GPU demand.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: AMD CEO Lisa Su used an October 6 press session in Taipei to signal that the company will substantially expand chip supply in 2027. "We've been able to increase our supply as we've gone through 2026, and we're going to substantially increase our supply in 2027," Su told reporters. She did not disclose a revised production target or product-level allocation, but she said AMD is extending joint capacity planning with its wafer, packaging, substrate, and memory partners from a one- or two-year horizon to a three- to five-year horizon. Her Taiwan stop reaffirmed the previously announced plan to invest more than $10 billion into Taiwan's industrial ecosystem, and included meetings with Foxconn and TSMC before a South Korea leg to see Samsung and SK hynix.

The capacity-planning change is the actual news. The usual AI-chip conversation is denominated in gigawatts of eventual data-center capacity and headline multi-year deals — the OpenAI, Meta, and Oracle commitments announced at Advancing AI 2026 in July are examples. Those deals do not come true unless the long-lead inputs line up on the same calendar: wafers from TSMC, HBM4 from the Korean memory makers, advanced packaging from a limited set of OSAT suppliers, substrates, thermal modules, and server assembly from Foxconn and its peers. Moving from a one- or two-year to a three- to five-year joint plan is AMD acknowledging that an Instinct GPU is not a thing you can double-ship on a quarter's notice.

Su also pointed directly at agentic and enterprise AI as the demand driver. That is a shift in framing. For much of the last two years, the demand story for AI accelerators has been dominated by frontier-model training runs — a small number of extremely large customers, each buying tens of thousands of GPUs for one project. Agentic workloads are the inverse: many customers, serving many concurrent agents to many users, each agent making many short inference calls. That shape of demand puts pressure on inference-friendly GPUs, on CPUs for orchestration, and especially on memory bandwidth, which is why Su spent time on HBM supply and described memory supply as tight across the market.

A takeaway for learners: when a chip CEO changes planning horizons, that is more informative than a dollar figure in a press release. A five-year joint plan with suppliers is a bet that the demand curve for AI compute keeps rising long enough for those commitments to clear. It is also an implicit admission that the near-term bottleneck is not design but industrial capacity — the physical ability to produce more wafers, package them, and ship servers. For anyone trying to understand why a given AI product feels gated by waitlists and quota rather than by what the model can do, this is the sentence that explains it.
